items.memo:
BILL NUMBER:  S5296

 TITLE OF BILL :  An act to amend the administrative code of the city
of New York, the emergency tenant protection act of nineteen
seventy-four, and the emergency housing rent control law, in relation
to adjustment of maximum allowable rent

 PURPOSE OR GENERAL IDEA OF THE BILL : Expenses for individual
apartment improvements in rental housing are currently recovered over
three and a half years in calculating the permissible monthly rent
increase.  This bill increases the length of time to seven years and
authorizes the Division of Housing and Community Renewal (DHCR) to
approve such rent increases for vacant apartments.

 SUMMARY OF SPECIFIC PROVISIONS :  Sections 1 through 4 increase the
amortization period for expenses due to individual apartment increases
from 40 months to 84 months.

Section 2 provides that no rent increase shall be collectible for an
individual apartment improvement unless:

* the owner of the apartment has provided the tenant with a lease
rider explaining how the rent in the vacancy lease has been computed;

* there are no current hazardous violations of any municipal, county,
State or Federal law that relate to the maintenance of any required
services;

* there are no outstanding determination by the DHCR that the owner
has failed to maintain any required services;

* the owner of the apartment has filed an explanation of how the
vacancy rent was computed, that exceeds 20 percent of the rent charged
to the previous tenant including supporting documentation.

 EFFECTS OF PRESENT LAW WHICH THIS BILL WOULD ALTER :  Extends the
amortization period from 40 months to 84 months and gives DHCR a
stronger oversight role by authorizing it to approve or disapprove
increases in whole or in part.

 JUSTIFICATION : There is a major loophole in the rent regulation
system called the 1/40th loophole, also known as an Individual
Apartment Improvement Increase. This loophole allows a landlord to
raise the rent on an unoccupied rent Stabilized apartment by passing
the cost of physical improvements to the next tenant by raising the
monthly rent an amount equal to 1/40th of the total cost of the
improvements.  A 1/40th increase can be taken in addition to any other
rent increase to which the landlord is statutorily entitled. There is
no oversight of any kind of the 1/40th loophole. Landlords are allowed
to unilaterally impose I/40th rent increases without prior approval,
or even documentation.

This lack of oversight has led to widespread fraud, and has been a
major reason for the loss of affordable housing in New York.
Landlords are able to use the 1/40th increase to move the apartment
above the current $2,000 High Rent Vacancy Decontrol threshold that
allows them to permanently de-regulate the apartment. Although there
are not absolutely clear government records of the frequency with
which 1/40th increases are used, because there is no oversight of the
program, it is clear that rent regulated apartments are moving out of
affordability at a rate faster than statutory rent increases would
allow.

Fraudulent rent increases for apartment renovations are a major reason
affordable housing is disappearing from New York, claims a recent

study by the Association for Neighborhood and Housing Development
(ANHD).

The oversight mechanism is an inadequate tenant-initiated.complaint
filed with DHCR as a Complaint of Rent Overcharge. Because the
improvement occurs in a vacant apartment, the new tenant has no way of
knowing what the rent should be, and if the work done justifies the
increase. This legislation would give DHCR the authority to approve or
disapprove such increases in whole or in part based upon the proof of
expenses submitted by the landlord.

 PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY : New legislation.

 FISCAL IMPLICATIONS :  Some administrative expense associated with
DHCR overseeing this program.

 EFFECTIVE DATE : Immediately.

A.memo:
BILL NUMBER:S5296A

TITLE OF BILL:
An act to amend the administrative code of the city of New York, the
emergency tenant protection act of nineteen seventy-four, and the emer-
gency housing rent control law, in relation to adjustment of maximum
allowable rent

PURPOSE OR GENERAL IDEA OF THE BILL:
Expenses for individual apartment improvements in rental housing are
currently recovered over three and a half years in calculating the
permissible monthly rent increase.  This bill increases the length of
time to five years and requires the Division of Housing and Community
Renewal (DHCR) to approve such rent increases for vacant apartments
which would increase the legal rent by more than ten percent. It also
would require owners to file exit registrations with DC", and give
notice to a new tenant after an apartment is Subject to vacancy decon-
trol stating the reason for deregulation and a calculation of how the
last rent was increased to exceed the $2,000 vacancy decontrol thresh-
old. The notice will also advise tenants as to how they can verify the
last legal regulated rent with DHCR.

SUMMARY OF SPECIFIC PROVISIONS:
Sections 1, 2, 4 and 5 increase the amortization period for expenses due
to individual apartment improvement increases from 40 months to 60
months.

Sections 2 and 4 provide that no rent increase shall be collectible for
an individual apartment improvement unless:

* the owner of the apartment has provided the tenant with.a lease rider
or a notice explaining in detail how the individual apartment improve-
ment rent increase in the vacancy lease has been computed;

* there are no current hazardous violations of any municipal, county,
State or Federal law that relate to the maintenance of any required
services;

* there is no outstanding determination by the DHCR that the owner has
failed to maintain any required services;

* the owner of the apartment has filed with DHCR an explanation and
documentation of how the individual apartment improvement rent increase
was computed, whenever such rent exceeds 10 percent of the rent charged
to the previous tenant including supporting documentation.  A new tenant
must be given an opportunity to respond to the owner's filing with the
DHCR prior to the DHCR's determination of the appropriate rent increase.

Section 3 provides that vacancy lease riders given to rent stabilized
tenants in New York City must include detailed breakdowns of any indi-
vidual apartment improvement rent increase charged to the new tenant.

Sections 6 and 7 require owners to file "exit" registrations with DHCR
and give notices to the first tenant after an apartment is subject to
vacancy decontrol stating the reason for deregulation and a calculation
of how the last rent was increased to exceed the $2,000 vacancy decon-
trol threshold.  The notice will also advise tenants as to how they can
verify the last legal regulated rent with DHCR.

These sections also stipulate that units cannot leave rent regulation
unless and until an "exit" registration is filed with DHCR and copies of
the registration and the notice of how the apartment was subjected to
vacancy deregulation are served upon the new tenant.

EFFECTS OF PRESENT LAW WHICH THIS BILL WOULD ALTER:
Extends the amortization period from 40 months to 60 months and gives
DHCR a stronger oversight role by authorizing it to approve or disap-
prove larger rent increases in whole or in part.

JUSTIFICATION:
There is a major loophole in the rent regulation system called the
1/40th loophole, also known as an Individual Apartment Improvement
Increase. This loophole allows a landlord to raise the rent on an unoc-
cupied rent stabilized apartment by passing the cost of physical
improvements to the next tenant by raising the monthly rent an amount
equal to 1/40th of the total cost of the improvements.  A 1/40th
increase can be taken in addition to any other rent increase to which
the landlord is statutorily entitled. There is no oversight of any kind
of the 1/40th loophole. Landlords are allowed to unilaterally impose
1/40th rent increases without prior approval, or even documentation.

This lack of oversight has led to widespread fraud, and has been a major
reason for the loss of affordable housing in New York.  Landlords are
able to use the 1/40th increase to move the apartment above the current
$2,000 High Rent Vacancy Decontrol threshold that allows them to perma-
nently de-regulate the apartment. Although there are not absolutely
clear government records of the frequency with which 1/40th increases
are used, because there is no oversight of the program, it is clear that
rent regulated apartments are moving out of affordability at a rate
faster than statutory rent increases would allow.

Fraudulent rent increases for apartment renovations are a major reason
affordable housing is disappearing from New York, according to a recent
study by the Association for Neighborhood and Housing Development
(ANHD).

The only present oversight mechanism is an inadequate tenant-initiated
complaint filed with DHCR as a Complaint of Rent Overcharge. Because the
improvement occurs in a vacant. apartment, the new tenant has no way of
knowing what the rent should be, and if the work done justifies the
increase.

This legislation would give DHCR the authority to approve or disapprove
such increases in whole or in part based upon the proof of expenses

submitted by the landlord. It will also give new tenants a breakdown of
how their rents are computed and information allowing them to challenge
such rents.

PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:
New legislation.

FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:
Some expense associated with DHCR administration of this program.

EFFECTIVE DATE:
This act takes effect on the 90th day after it becomes law except that
sections six and seven take effect on the 30th day after the it becomes
law and DHCR is authorized and directed to promulgate rules, regu-
lations, and standards immediately.
